record.paper_title: Open Problems in Data-Sharing Peer-to-Peer Systems
record.original_question: How can ranked-search techniques for distributed systems be extended so that they remain effective at the much larger scales expected in peer-to-peer data-sharing systems, while still exploiting the possibility of returning only the top k results instead of the full result set?

evidence.quote: Techniques for ranked search exists for distributed systems of moderate scale (e.g., [7]), but future research must extend these techniques to support much larger systems.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a distributed data-sharing network modeled as a set of N nodes, each holding a local document collection, where N can be very large (e.g., 10^6 or more). Each document d has, for each query q drawn from some query space Q, a real-valued relevance score s(d,q). A ranked-search protocol is an algorithm that, given a query q issued at one node, returns the k documents in the entire network with the highest scores s(d,q), for a user-specified parameter k much smaller than the total number of relevant documents.

Design a ranked-search protocol for this setting that simultaneously achieves the following properties as N grows:

1. Correctness: with high probability the returned set equals (or has bounded approximation ratio to) the true global top-k by score s(·,q).
2. Scalability: the per-node communication, computation, and storage cost grows sublinearly (ideally polylogarithmically) in N, and the total network traffic per query is asymptotically smaller than the cost of retrieving the full result set.
3. Top-k exploitation: the protocol must take essential advantage of the bound k, so that its cost depends on k and decreases substantially when k is small compared to retrieving all matching documents.
4. Robustness: the protocol should remain effective under node churn, heterogeneous node capacities, and skewed score and document distributions across nodes.

Provide such a protocol and prove matching upper and lower bounds on its communication complexity as a function of N, k, and the score distribution, or prove that no protocol can simultaneously achieve all four properties.
artifact.category_tag: Distributed top-k ranked search in peer-to-peer systems
artifact.status_search_result: The question concerns scaling distributed ranked-search/top-k retrieval to very large peer-to-peer networks. A substantial body of work (e.g., on distributed top-k algorithms such as TPUT, KLEE, and DHT-based ranked retrieval) has produced partial solutions and approximations, but no single protocol is known to optimally combine scalability, top-k exploitation, and robustness under realistic peer-to-peer conditions. The status as a precisely posed mathematical problem is not definitively resolved in the literature surveyed.

status_evidence.title: Efficient top-k query processing in distributed networks (KLEE)
status_evidence.snippet: KLEE provides approximate top-k retrieval in distributed peer-to-peer systems with reduced communication cost compared to exact methods.
status_evidence.claim: Partial solutions for scalable distributed top-k retrieval exist, but trade off accuracy for cost.

status_evidence.title: Optimal aggregation algorithms for middleware (Fagin, Lotem, Naor)
status_evidence.snippet: Provides threshold-style algorithms for top-k retrieval over multiple sources with instance optimality results.
status_evidence.claim: Foundational top-k algorithms are known but were designed for moderate-scale distributed settings.
